evidence_set: Cases in which people believed they had taken LSD: a 24-year-old woman at the Burning Man festival had taken 'acid' on blotter paper, whose remains held mainly 25C-NBOMe and a very small amount of 25I-NBOMe; her own samples were not analysed. Three people in Belgium, brought to hospital from the same party, reported using 'synthetic LSD'; 25I-NBOMe was confirmed in their urine, with no other drugs detected. A 21-year-old man in Houston who reportedly had taken two 'hits of acid' and smoked cannabis hallucinated, reportedly injured himself, attacked a friend, and was found unresponsive; 25I-NBOMe and cannabis metabolites were found in his post-mortem heart blood and urine. A 19-year-old in Richmond, Virginia, 'trip sitting' friends who were reportedly using 'acid', behaved strangely and was found after probably jumping or falling from a balcony; a case-related sample of unused blotter paper held 25I-NBOMe and targeted analysis found it in his blood, urine, brain, liver and bile; his friends did not know he had taken anything, and those who took the 'acid' blotters showed no similar symptoms. In Belgium a person had used a blotter at a party that they thought contained LSD; no LSD was found, and analytical confirmation of 25I-NBOMe was not reported.

Editors' count from the case descriptions: the NBOMe was found in the patient's own samples, with the result linked to the patient, in 15 of the 29 published cases (both Hong Kong cases, the Richmond 25B-NBOMe case, the seven Hill cases, the Richmond 25I-NBOMe case, the St Paul case and three of the four Grand Rapids cases); only the product was analysed in 2 (Detroit, Burning Man); no analysis linked to the patient was reported in 12 (the German 25C-NBOMe case, the ten Richmond patients, whose two analysed serum samples could not be linked to patients, and one Grand Rapids patient). Other drugs found or reported include amphetamine and methamphetamine in six of the seven Hill cases, ketamine in the second Hong Kong case, caffeine in three Grand Rapids cases, a substance thought to be a phencyclidine analogue in the Detroit eye dropper, and co-use reported by four of the ten Richmond patients. The Conclusions say only some reports included analytical confirmation, read the features as both serotonin syndrome and sympathomimetic toxicity, much like MDMA, certain other amphetamines and mephedrone, and say the significance of post-mortem detection for the deaths has often not been determined.

evidence_set: Figure 5 (laboratory-analysed tablets sold as ecstasy, 1993–2010) shows two periods when many tablets held other substances instead of or besides MDMA: around 1997 (amphetamines) and around 2009 (mCPP). The authors state that only 30% of tablets handed in during October 1997 contained MDMA or an MDMA-like substance, and only 40% in March 2009 contained MDMA; these monthly lows have no denominators, and the yearly figure cannot confirm them.
